title: When Consensus Decision-Making Strangles an Organization
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay critiques the widespread organizational default of consensus decision-making, acknowledging its value for buy-in and collaboration while arguing it frequently becomes a mechanism for paralysis. It describes how including too many stakeholders and gathering too many opinions can make decisions functionally impossible to finalize, letting self-interested parties stall progress indefinitely. Its proposed fix is structural: naming a designated Decision-Maker for every major decision with a deadline, so that if consensus isn't reached in time, someone with authority makes the call -- which the piece argues also creates urgency that often produces consensus anyway.
points: Consensus decision-making fosters buy-in and collaboration but can also let self-interested stakeholders stall or stonewall decisions.
Including too many stakeholders and gathering too many opinions can make full agreement functionally impossible to reach.
When decisions languish, opportunities are lost and team members grow frustrated waiting for resolution.
The recommended fix is naming a designated Decision-Maker with a deadline, who makes the call if consensus isn't reached in time.
Knowing a decision will be taken out of their hands by a deadline often creates the urgency stakeholders need to reach consensus on their own.
quotes: Consensus can be a powerful standard for making quality decisions and encouraging vigorous execution.
Unfortunately, in many organizations, it also prevents decisions from ever happening.
With so many varied views and opinions, finding common ground and getting everyone to agree with a decision is nearly impossible.
Someone must be able to break the logjam of indecision when building consensus doesn't lead to a decision. Naming a Decision-Maker for every major decision is key.

When team members know a decision will be pried from their hands if they don't reach consensus by a specific date, they typically find the urgency to establish common ground before they run out of time.
Consensus decision-making should never lead to nothing. A designated Decision-Maker prevents a bad process from holding an organization hostage.
